excerpt: Your claim survives the at-fault driver's death. How to pursue it in Georgia or South Carolina through insurance, the estate, or your own coverage.
keyTakeaways: Your right to compensation does not disappear when the at-fault driver dies. Georgia (O.C.G.A. § 9-2-41) and South Carolina (S.C. Code § 15-5-90) both allow personal injury claims to survive the tortfeasor's death. You can pursue the claim through the driver's liability insurance, a lawsuit against their estate, or your own UM/UIM coverage. Filing deadlines are two years in Georgia (O.C.G.A. § 9-3-33) and three in South Carolina (S.C. Code § 15-3-530), and the driver's death can pause those clocks (O.C.G.A. § 9-3-93; S.C. Code § 62-3-802(b)), but any recovery beyond the driver's insurance must also be presented as a probate claim, in South Carolina within the earlier of one year after death or eight months after notice to creditors (S.C. Code § 62-3-803).

faqs.question: Can I still file a personal injury claim if the at-fault driver died in the accident?
faqs.answer: Yes. In both Georgia (O.C.G.A. § 9-2-41) and South Carolina (S.C. Code § 15-5-90), personal injury claims survive the death of the at-fault party. You can pursue compensation through the deceased driver's liability insurance, a lawsuit against their estate, or your own uninsured/underinsured motorist coverage.

faqs.question: Do I sue the deceased driver's family members?
faqs.answer: No. You sue the personal representative of the deceased driver's estate (the executor or administrator appointed by the probate court) in that capacity, not the family members personally. In Georgia an estate is not itself a legal entity that can be sued (Orange County Trust Co. v. Estate of Takowsky, 1969; O.C.G.A. § 9-2-41), and in South Carolina the proceeding is against the personal representative (S.C. Code § 62-3-804). The deceased driver's liability insurance typically defends the case and pays any judgment up to policy limits. Family members' personal assets are generally not at risk unless they owned or furnished the vehicle (the family purpose doctrine) or were independently negligent.

faqs.question: What if the deceased driver had no insurance or not enough coverage?
faqs.answer: If the deceased driver was uninsured or underinsured, you may file a claim through your own uninsured/underinsured motorist (UM/UIM) coverage. To reach the estate's assets, you may also present a claim in the probate proceeding and sue the personal representative. An attorney can identify all available sources of recovery to maximize your compensation.

faqs.question: How long do I have to file a claim against a deceased at-fault driver?
faqs.answer: The standard statutes of limitations apply — two years in Georgia (O.C.G.A. § 9-3-33) and three years in South Carolina (S.C. Code § 15-3-530) — and the driver's death can pause them (Georgia: up to five years while the estate has no personal representative, O.C.G.A. § 9-3-93; South Carolina: eight months after death, S.C. Code § 62-3-802(b)). To reach the estate's own assets beyond the insurance, present a probate claim: in South Carolina within the earlier of one year after death or eight months after the first published notice to creditors (S.C. Code § 62-3-803(a)), a bar that does not apply to the insured part of the claim (S.C. Code § 62-3-803(d)(2)); in Georgia, notify the personal representative within three months of the last published notice (O.C.G.A. § 53-7-41). Consult an attorney promptly to avoid missing any deadlines.

faqs.question: Is it wrong to pursue a claim when the other driver has died?
faqs.answer: Your claim is primarily against the insurance company, not the deceased driver's family. Auto insurance exists for this exact purpose — the at-fault driver paid premiums so their insurer would cover damages from their negligence. Your medical bills, lost wages, and suffering are real regardless of the other driver's fate, and not pursuing the claim only leaves you bearing the full financial burden.

faqs.question: What evidence challenges arise when the at-fault driver is deceased?
faqs.answer: The deceased driver cannot testify, which means the insurance company may try to shift blame onto you without contradiction. This makes objective evidence critical: police reports, witness statements, dashcam footage, accident reconstruction analysis, cell phone records, and toxicology reports from the autopsy can all help establish fault in the absence of the other driver's testimony.
